'''Food technology''' is a branch of [[food science]] that addresses the production, preservation, quality control and research and development of food products.

It may also be understood as the science of ensuring that a society is food secure and has access to safe food that meets quality standards.<ref>Campbell-Platt, Geoffrey, ed. Food science and technology. John Wiley & Sons, 2017.</ref>

Early [[Food science|scientific research]] into food technology concentrated on [[food preservation]]. [[Nicolas Appert]]'s development in 1810 of the [[canning]] process was a decisive event. The process wasn't called canning then and Appert did not really know the principle on which his process worked, but canning has had a major impact on food preservation techniques<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Did We Can? {{!}} About |url=https://www.nal.usda.gov/exhibits/ipd/canning/about |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=www.nal.usda.gov}}</ref>.

[[Louis Pasteur]]'s research on the spoilage of [[wine]] and his description of how to avoid spoilage in 1864, was an early attempt to apply scientific knowledge to food handling. Besides research into [[wine spoilage]], Pasteur researched the production of [[ethanol|alcohol]], [[vinegar]], wines and [[beer]], and the [[Soured milk|souring of milk]]. He developed [[pasteurization]] – the process of heating milk and milk products to destroy food spoilage and disease-producing [[microorganisms|organisms]]. In his research into food technology, Pasteur became the pioneer into [[bacteria|bacteriology]] and of modern [[Preventive healthcare|preventive medicine]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=History's Hunger Heroes: Louis Pasteur |url=https://wfpusa.org/news/historys-hunger-heroes-louis-pasteur/ |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=World Food Program USA |language=en-US}}</ref>.

== Developments ==
[[File:Liofilizat 04 pl.jpg|thumb|right|[[Freeze-drying|Freeze-dried]] [[coffee]], a form of [[instant coffee]]]]

Developments in food technology have contributed greatly to the food supply and have changed our world. Some of these developments are: 
* [[Powdered milk|Instantized milk powder]] – Instant milk powder has become the basis for a variety of new products that are rehydratable. This process increases the [[surface area]] of the powdered product by partially rehydrating spray-dried milk powder.
* [[Freeze-drying]] – The first application of freeze drying was most likely in the [[pharmaceutical]] industry; however, a successful large-scale industrial application of the process was the development of continuous freeze drying of coffee.
* [[Ultra-high temperature processing|High-temperature short time processing]] – These processes, for the most part, are characterized by rapid heating and cooling, holding for a short time at a relatively high temperature and filling aseptically into [[Sterilization (microbiology)|sterile]] containers.
* [[Decaffeination]] of [[coffee]] and [[tea]] – Decaffeinated coffee and tea was first developed on a commercial basis in [[Europe]] around 1900. The process is described in U.S. patent 897,763. Green coffee beans are treated with water, heat and [[solvent]]s to remove the caffeine from the beans. 
* [[Process optimization]] – Food technology now allows production of foods to be more efficient, oil saving technologies are now available on different forms. Production methods and [[methodology]] have also become increasingly sophisticated.
*[[Aseptic processing|Aseptic packaging]] – the process of filling a commercially sterile product into a sterile container and hermetically sealing the containers so that re-infection is prevented. Thus, this results into a shelf stable product at ambient conditions.
* [[Food irradiation]] – the process of exposing food and food packaging to ionizing radiation can effectively destroy organisms responsible for spoilage and foodborne illness and inhibit sprouting, extending shelf life.
*Commercial fruit ripening rooms using [[ethylene as a plant hormone]].
* [[Food delivery]] – An order is typically made either through a restaurant or grocer's website or mobile app, or through a food ordering company. The ordered food is typically delivered in boxes or bags to the customer's doorsteps.

==Categories==

Technology has innovated these categories from the [[food industry]]:<ref>{{cite web|title=What is FoodTech?|url=https://www.digitalfoodlab.com/foodtech|website=digitalfoodlab.com|access-date=20 January 2022}}</ref>
* [[Agricultural technology]] – or AgTech, it is the use of technology in [[agriculture]], [[horticulture]], and [[aquaculture]] with the aim of improving yield, efficiency, and profitability. Agricultural technology can be products, services or applications derived from agriculture that improve various input/output processes.
* [[Food science]] –  technology in this sector focuses on the development of new functional ingredients and alternative Proteins.
* [[Foodservice]] – technology innovated the way establishments prepare, supply, and serve food outside the home.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Firsthand|url=https://firsthand.co/industries/restaurants-and-food-services/background|access-date=2022-01-25|website=firsthand.co}}</ref> There's a tendency to create the conditions for the restaurant of the future with [[robotics]] and [[CloudKitchens]].
* Consumer Tech – technology allows what we call [[consumer electronics]], which is the equipment of consumers with devices that facilitates the cooking process. 
*[[Food delivery]] –  as the food delivery [[Market (economics)|market]] is growing, [[companies]] and [[startups]] are rapidly revolutionizing the communication process between consumers and food establishments, with platform-to-consumer delivery as the global lead.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Online Food Delivery – Worldwide {{!}} Statista Market Forecast|url=https://www.statista.com/outlook/dmo/eservices/online-food-delivery/worldwide|access-date=2022-01-25|website=Statista|language=en}}</ref>
* [[Supply chain]] – supply chain activities are considerably moving from [[digitization]] to [[automation]].

==Emerging technologies==

[[Innovation]] in the food sector may include, for example, new types for raw [[Materials Processing|material processing]] [[technology]], [[Packaging and labeling|packaging]] of products, and new [[food additive]]s. Applying new solutions may reduce or prevent adverse changes caused by [[microorganism]]s, oxidation of food ingredients, and enzymatic and nonenzymatic reactions. Moreover, healthier and more nutritious food may be delivered as well as the food may [[taste]] better due to improvements in food composition, including organoleptic changes, and changes in the perception and pleasures from eating food.<ref>M. Klimczuk-Kochańska, A. Klimczuk, ''Innovation in Food and Agriculture'', [in:] P.B. Thompson, D.M. Kaplan (eds.), ''Encyclopedia of Food and Agricultural Ethics'', Second Edition, Springer, Dordrecht 2018, pp. 1-7, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-007-6167-4_628-1.</ref>

In the 21st century, emerging technologies such as [[cellular agriculture]], particularly [[cultured meat]], [[3D food printing]], use of [[insect protein]], [[Meat alternative|plant-based alternative]]s, [[vertical farming]], [[food delivery|food deliveries]] and [[blockchain technology]] are being developed to accelerate the transformation towards sustainable food systems.<ref>{{cite news|title=Insect consumption|work=BBC News |date=12 July 2012 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-18813075|access-date=5 May 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bunge |first1=A. Charlotte |last2=Wood |first2=Amanda |last3=Halloran |first3=Afton |last4=Gordon |first4=Line J. |title=A systematic scoping review of the sustainability of vertical farming, plant-based alternatives, food delivery services and blockchain in food systems |journal=[[Nature Food]] |date=2022 |volume=3 |issue=11 |pages=933–941 |doi=10.1038/s43016-022-00622-8 |doi-access=free|pmid=37118205 }}</ref>

=== Alternative protein sources ===
With the global population expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050,<ref>{{Cite web |title=World Population Prospects – Population Division – United Nations |url=https://population.un.org/wpp/ |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=population.un.org}}</ref> there is an urgent need for alternative protein sources that are sustainable, nutritious, and environmentally friendly. Plant-based proteins are gaining popularity as they require fewer resources and produce fewer greenhouse gas emissions compared to animal-based proteins.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Poore |first1=J. |last2=Nemecek |first2=T. |year=2018 |title=Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers |journal=Science |volume=360 |issue=6392 |pages=987–992 |doi=10.1126/science.aaq0216 |pmid=29853680}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The market for alternative protein: Pea protein, cultured meat, and more {{!}} McKinsey |url=https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/agriculture/our-insights/alternative-proteins-the-race-for-market-share-is-on |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=mckinsey.com |archive-date=22 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322153542/https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/agriculture/our-insights/alternative-proteins-the-race-for-market-share-is-on |url-status=dead }}</ref> Companies like Beyond Meat and Impossible Foods have developed plant-based meat alternatives that mimic the taste and texture of traditional meat products.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A growing population calls for sustainable protein – EIT Food |url=https://www.eitfood.eu/blog/a-growing-population-calls-for-sustainable-protein |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=eitfood.eu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Nutrients |url=https://www.mdpi.com/journal/nutrients/special_issues/Beyond_Meat_Alternative_Sources_of_Proteins_to_Feed_the_World |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=mdpi.com |language=en}}</ref>

=== Food waste reduction ===
Approximately one-third of all food produced globally is wasted.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Quinton |first=Amy M. |date=2019-10-01 |title=Why Is One-Third of Our Food Wasted Worldwide? |url=https://www.ucdavis.edu/food/news/why-is-one-third-our-food-wasted-worldwide |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=UC Davis |language=en |archive-date=22 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322153659/https://www.ucdavis.edu/food/news/why-is-one-third-our-food-wasted-worldwide |url-status=dead }}</ref> Innovative food tech solutions are being developed to address this issue. For example, Apeel Sciences has developed an edible coating that extends the shelf life of fruits and vegetables, reducing spoilage and waste.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Apeel Sciences {{!}} WFP Innovation |url=https://innovation.wfp.org/project/apeel-sciences |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=innovation.wfp.org |language=en |archive-date=22 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322153711/https://innovation.wfp.org/project/apeel-sciences |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Consumer acceptance ==

Historically, consumers paid little attention to food technologies. Nowadays, the [[food production]] chain is long and complicated and food technologies are diverse. Consequently, consumers are uncertain about the determinants of [[food quality]] and find it difficult to understand them. Now, acceptance of food products very often depends on perceived benefits and risks associated with food. Popular views of food processing technologies matter.  Especially innovative food processing technologies often are perceived as risky by consumers.<ref>Ueland Ö, G. H., Holm, F., Kalogeras, N., Leino, O., Luteijn, J., Magnusson, S.(2011). State of the art in benefit-risk analysis: Consumer perception. Food and Chemical Toxicology, 52(1)</ref>
 
Acceptance of the different food technologies varies. While pasteurization is well recognized and accepted, high pressure treatment and even microwaves often are perceived as risky. Studies by the Hightech Europe project found that traditional technologies were well accepted in contrast to innovative technologies.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hightecheurope.eu/documents.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121205013216/http://www.hightecheurope.eu/documents.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-12-05 |title=Documents |publisher=Hightecheurope.eu |access-date=2014-02-01 }}</ref>

Consumers form their attitude towards innovative food technologies through three main mechanisms: First, through knowledge or beliefs about risks and benefits correlated with the technology; second, through attitudes based on their own experience; and third, through application of higher order values and beliefs.<ref>Olsen, N. V., Grunert, K.G., & Anne-Mette, S. (2010). Consumer acceptance of high-pressure processing and pulsed-electric field: a review. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 21(446–472)</ref>
A number of scholars consider the risk-benefit trade-off as one of the main determinants of consumer acceptance,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Frewer|first1=Lynn J.|last2=van der Lans|first2=Ivo A.|last3=Fischer|first3=Arnout R.H.|last4=Reinders|first4=Machiel J.|last5=Menozzi|first5=Davide|last6=Zhang|first6=Xiaoyong|last7=van den Berg|first7=Isabelle|last8=Zimmermann|first8=Karin L.|title=Public perceptions of agri-food applications of genetic modification – A systematic review and meta-analysis|journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology|date=April 2013|volume=30|issue=2|pages=142–152|doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2013.01.003|hdl=11381/2561244|hdl-access=free}}</ref> although some researchers place more emphasis on the role of benefit perception (rather than risk) in consumer acceptance.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gaskell|first1=George|last2=Allum|first2=Nick|last3=Wagner|first3=Wolfgang|last4=Kronberger|first4=Nicole|last5=Torgersen|first5=Helge|last6=Hampel|first6=Juergen|last7=Bardes|first7=Julie|title=GM Foods and the Misperception of Risk Perception|journal=Risk Analysis|date=February 2004|volume=24|issue=1|pages=185–194|doi=10.1111/j.0272-4332.2004.00421.x|pmid=15028010|bibcode=2004RiskA..24..185G |s2cid=41150301 |url=http://hw.oeaw.ac.at/?arp=ita/ita-papers/HT_04_1.pdf}}</ref>

Rogers (2010) defines five major criteria that explain differences in the acceptance of new technology by consumers: complexity, compatibility, relative advantage, trialability and observability.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Rogers|first1=Everett M.|title=Diffusion of Innovations|date=2010|publisher=Free Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0743222099|edition=5|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/diffusionofinnov00roge}}</ref>

Acceptance of innovative technologies can be improved by providing non-emotional and concise information about these new technological processes methods. The HighTech project also suggests that written information has a higher impact on consumers than audio-visual information.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hightecheurope.eu/documents.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121205013216/http://www.hightecheurope.eu/documents.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-12-05 |title=Documents |publisher=Hightecheurope.eu |access-date=2014-02-01 }}</ref>

'''Food technology''' is a branch of [[food science]] that addresses the production, preservation, quality control and research and development of food products.

It may also be understood as the science of ensuring that a society is food secure and has access to safe food that meets quality standards.<ref>Campbell-Platt, Geoffrey, ed. Food science and technology. John Wiley & Sons, 2017.</ref>

Early [[Food science|scientific research]] into food technology concentrated on [[food preservation]]. [[Nicolas Appert]]'s development in 1810 of the [[canning]] process was a decisive event. The process wasn't called canning then and Appert did not really know the principle on which his process worked, but canning has had a major impact on food preservation techniques<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Did We Can? {{!}} About |url=https://www.nal.usda.gov/exhibits/ipd/canning/about |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=www.nal.usda.gov}}</ref>.

[[Louis Pasteur]]'s research on the spoilage of [[wine]] and his description of how to avoid spoilage in 1864, was an early attempt to apply scientific knowledge to food handling. Besides research into [[wine spoilage]], Pasteur researched the production of [[ethanol|alcohol]], [[vinegar]], wines and [[beer]], and the [[Soured milk|souring of milk]]. He developed [[pasteurization]] – the process of heating milk and milk products to destroy food spoilage and disease-producing [[microorganisms|organisms]]. * [[Decaffeination]] of [[coffee]] and [[tea]] – Decaffeinated coffee and tea was first developed on a commercial basis in [[Europe]] around 1900. The process is described in U.S. patent 897,763. Green coffee beans are treated with water, heat and [[solvent]]s to remove the caffeine from the beans. 
* [[Process optimization]] – Food technology now allows production of foods to be more efficient, oil saving technologies are now available on different forms. Production methods and [[methodology]] have also become increasingly sophisticated.

The process wasn't called canning then and Appert did not really know the principle on which his process worked, but canning has had a major impact on food preservation techniques<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Did We Can? {{!}} About |url=https://www.nal.usda.gov/exhibits/ipd/canning/about |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=www.nal.usda.gov}}</ref>.

[[Louis Pasteur]]'s research on the spoilage of [[wine]] and his description of how to avoid spoilage in 1864, was an early attempt to apply scientific knowledge to food handling. Besides research into [[wine spoilage]], Pasteur researched the production of [[ethanol|alcohol]], [[vinegar]], wines and [[beer]], and the [[Soured milk|souring of milk]]. He developed [[pasteurization]] – the process of heating milk and milk products to destroy food spoilage and disease-producing [[microorganisms|organisms]]. Green coffee beans are treated with water, heat and [[solvent]]s to remove the caffeine from the beans.

Early [[Food science|scientific research]] into food technology concentrated on [[food preservation]]. [[Nicolas Appert]]'s development in 1810 of the [[canning]] process was a decisive event. The process wasn't called canning then and Appert did not really know the principle on which his process worked, but canning has had a major impact on food preservation techniques.

[[Louis Pasteur]]'s research on the spoilage of [[wine]] and his description of how to avoid spoilage in 1864, was an early attempt to apply scientific knowledge to food handling. Besides research into [[wine spoilage]], Pasteur researched the production of [[ethanol|alcohol]], [[vinegar]], wines and [[beer]], and the [[Soured milk|souring of milk]]. He developed [[pasteurization]] – the process of heating milk and milk products to destroy food spoilage and disease-producing [[microorganisms|organisms]]. * [[Ultra-high temperature processing|High-Temperature Short Time Processing]] – These processes, for the most part, are characterized by rapid heating and cooling, holding for a short time at a relatively high temperature and filling aseptically into [[Sterilization (microbiology)|sterile]] containers.
* [[Decaffeination]] of [[Coffee]] and [[Tea]] – Decaffeinated coffee and tea was first developed on a commercial basis in [[Europe]] around 1900. The process is described in U.S. patent 897,763. Green coffee beans are treated with water, heat and [[solvent]]s to remove the caffeine from the beans. 
* [[Process optimization]] – Food Technology now allows production of foods to be more efficient, Oil saving technologies are now available on different forms. Production methods and [[methodology]] have also become increasingly sophisticated.
*[[Aseptic processing|Aseptic packaging]] – the process of filling a commercially sterile product into a sterile container and hermetically sealing the containers so that re-infection is prevented. Thus, this results into a shelf stable product at ambient conditions.
* [[Food irradiation]] – the process of exposing food and food packaging to ionizing radiation can effectively destroy organisms responsible for spoilage and foodborne illness and inhibit sprouting, extending shelf life.

* [[Food delivery]] – An order is typically made either through a restaurant or grocer's website or mobile app, or through a food ordering company. The ordered food is typically delivered in boxes or bags to the customer's doorsteps.

Plant-based proteins are gaining popularity as they require fewer resources and produce fewer greenhouse gas emissions compared to animal-based proteins.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The market for alternative protein: Pea protein, cultured meat, and more {{!}} McKinsey |url=https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/agriculture/our-insights/alternative-proteins-the-race-for-market-share-is-on |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=mckinsey.com}}</ref> Companies like Beyond Meat and Impossible Foods have developed plant-based meat alternatives that mimic the taste and texture of traditional meat products.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A growing population calls for sustainable protein – EIT Food |url=https://www.eitfood.eu/blog/a-growing-population-calls-for-sustainable-protein |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=eitfood.eu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Nutrients |url=https://www.mdpi.com/journal/nutrients/special_issues/Beyond_Meat_Alternative_Sources_of_Proteins_to_Feed_the_World |access-date=2023-03-22 |website=mdpi.com |language=en}}</ref>

== Consumer acceptance ==

Historically, consumers paid little attention to food technologies. Nowadays, the [[food production]] chain is long and complicated and food technologies are diverse. Consequently, consumers are uncertain about the determinants of [[food quality]] and find it difficult to understand them. Now, acceptance of food products very often depends on perceived benefits and risks associated with food. Popular views of food processing technologies matter.  Especially innovative food processing technologies often are perceived as risky by consumers.<ref>Ueland Ö, G. H., Holm, F., Kalogeras, N., Leino, O., Luteijn, J., Magnusson, S.(2011). State of the art in benefit-risk analysis: Consumer perception. Food and Chemical Toxicology, 52(1)</ref>
 
Acceptance of the different food technologies varies. While pasteurization is well recognized and accepted, high pressure treatment and even microwaves often are perceived as risky. Studies by the Hightech Europe project found that traditional technologies were well accepted in contrast to innovative technologies.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hightecheurope.eu/documents.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121205013216/http://www.hightecheurope.eu/documents.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-12-05 |title=Documents |publisher=Hightecheurope.eu |access-date=2014-02-01 }}</ref>

Consumers form their attitude towards innovative food technologies through three main mechanisms: First, through knowledge or beliefs about risks and benefits correlated with the technology; second, through attitudes based on their own experience; and third, through application of higher order values and beliefs.<ref>Olsen, N. V., Grunert, K.G., & Anne-Mette, S. (2010). Consumer acceptance of high-pressure processing and pulsed-electric field: a review. Trends in Food Science & Technology, 21(446–472)</ref>
A number of scholars consider the risk-benefit trade-off as one of the main determinants of consumer acceptance,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Frewer|first1=Lynn J.|last2=van der Lans|first2=Ivo A.|last3=Fischer|first3=Arnout R.H.|last4=Reinders|first4=Machiel J.|last5=Menozzi|first5=Davide|last6=Zhang|first6=Xiaoyong|last7=van den Berg|first7=Isabelle|last8=Zimmermann|first8=Karin L.|title=Public perceptions of agri-food applications of genetic modification – A systematic review and meta-analysis|journal=Trends in Food Science & Technology|date=April 2013|volume=30|issue=2|pages=142–152|doi=10.1016/j.tifs.2013.01.003|hdl=11381/2561244|hdl-access=free}}</ref> although some researchers place more emphasis on the role of benefit perception (rather than risk) in consumer acceptance.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gaskell|first1=George|last2=Allum|first2=Nick|last3=Wagner|first3=Wolfgang|last4=Kronberger|first4=Nicole|last5=Torgersen|first5=Helge|last6=Hampel|first6=Juergen|last7=Bardes|first7=Julie|title=GM Foods and the Misperception of Risk Perception|journal=Risk Analysis|date=February 2004|volume=24|issue=1|pages=185–194|doi=10.1111/j.0272-4332.2004.00421.x|pmid=15028010|bibcode=2004RiskA..24..185G |s2cid=41150301 |url=http://hw.oeaw.ac.at/?arp=ita/ita-papers/HT_04_1.pdf}}</ref>

Rogers (2010) defines five major criteria that explain differences in the acceptance of new technology by consumers: complexity, compatibility, relative advantage, trialability and observability.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Rogers|first1=Everett M.|title=Diffusion of Innovations|date=2010|publisher=Free Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0743222099|edition=5|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/diffusionofinnov00roge}}</ref>

Acceptance of innovative technologies can be improved by providing non-emotional and concise information about these new technological processes methods. The HighTech project also suggests that written information has a higher impact on consumers than audio-visual information.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hightecheurope.eu/documents.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121205013216/http://www.hightecheurope.eu/documents.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-12-05 |title=Documents |publisher=Hightecheurope.eu |access-date=2014-02-01 }}</ref>
